instrument.full_name: Declaration concerning the Prohibition of the Use of Bullets which Expand or Flatten Easily in the Human Body
instrument.adopted_at: The Hague, First International Peace Conference (question raised in the First Commission's first (military) subcommission, voted in the First Commission, adopted in plenary, and embodied in a separate act listed in the Final Act of 29 July 1899)
instrument.depositary: Government of the Netherlands. Ratifications are deposited at The Hague (operative para. 5), adhesions and denunciations are notified to the Netherlands Government (operative paras. 7 and 8), and the single original is kept in its archives (closing formula).
instrument.key_non_parties: The United States neither signed nor adhered. Its delegates, Captain Crozier and Mr White, opposed the text in the First Commission and in plenary, where it was adopted against the votes of the United States and Great Britain with Portugal abstaining (Proceedings, 1899, pp. 79-87, 276-280); the Dutch royal order of 23 January 1905 (FRUS 1905, doc. 704) marks the United States "neither signed nor ratified"; the depositary database and the ICRC list no United States entry; and Bevans, vol. 1, lists no expanding-bullet declaration. Great Britain and Portugal did not sign in 1899 but adhered on 30 and 29 August 1907 (Trb. 1966, 233; Scott 1915, p. 228). Most present-day states are not listed as parties; the depositary database lists 35 (checked 12 October 2026).
instrument.duration_clause: No term is stated. The undertaking to abstain (operative para. 1) is given without limit of time, unlike the five-year term of the sister Declaration (IV,1) on balloons. On 17 July 1899 the reporter's proposal to apply a five-year term to all three points was dropped after objections; Colonel Gilinsky (Russia) insisted that the bullet prohibition should continue indefinitely (Proceedings, 1899, pp. 324-325). Its application in a particular war depends on the general participation clause (operative paras. 2 and 3). The depositary records entry into force on 4 September 1900 and no termination.
instrument.withdrawal_clause: A High Contracting Party may denounce the Declaration by written notification to the Netherlands Government, which communicates it forthwith to the other Contracting Powers; the denunciation takes effect one year after the notification (operative para. 8) and affects only the notifying Power (operative para. 9). The engagement also ceases to be binding in a particular war once a non-contracting Power joins one of the belligerents (operative para. 3); that is a condition of application, not withdrawal. No denunciation is recorded in the depositary database.
instrument.entry_into_force_requirements: Ratification "as soon as possible" (operative para. 4), with ratifications deposited at The Hague and a proces-verbal drawn up on each deposit (operative paras. 5 and 6). The text sets no threshold and no entry-into-force date. The Netherlands Treaty Series (Trb. 1966, 233, section G) records that the Declaration entered into force on 4 September 1900 for the states that had ratified by that date and, for later ratifying or acceding states, on the dates of their deposit or accession. Non-signatory Powers may adhere by written notification to the Netherlands Government (operative para. 7); the text does not say when an adhesion takes effect.
instrument.count_basis: The Declaration has no numbered articles. Citations use: preamble (from "The undersigned" to the reference to the St Petersburg Declaration); operative paras. 1 to 9 (1 prohibition, 2 binding only between Contracting Powers, 3 cessation when a non-contracting Power joins, 4 ratification, 5 deposit at The Hague, 6 proces-verbal, 7 adhesion, 8 denunciation, 9 effect of denunciation); and the closing formula. Trb. 1966, 233 uses the same count ("alinea 5" for ratification, "alinea 7" for accession). Word count: authentic French text as reproduced by the ICRC (French page, read through its JSON:API), from "Les soussignés" to the end of the dating formula, excluding the title and "(Signatures)", whitespace tokenization with elided forms (e.g. d'être) counted as one word and the detached colon after "Déclarent" not counted: 325. The same procedure reproduces the 308 recorded for Declaration IV,2. Scott, Les Conventions et Déclarations de La Haye (1918), pp. 227-228, prints the St Petersburg date as "29 Novembre/11 Décembre" and "quatre-vingt" hyphenated, which gives 323 on the same basis. English: the local Avalon PDF (Scott translation), from "The Undersigned" to the end of the dating formula: 334 (ICRC English on the same basis: 332).
instrument.weapons_systems_limited: Bullets which expand or flatten easily in the human body, with two illustrations: bullets with a hard envelope which does not entirely cover the core, or which is pierced with incisions (operative para. 1). Delegates identified the British "dumdum" bullet made at the arsenal near Calcutta as the bullet in view, although the text does not name it (Proceedings, 1899, pp. 83-84, 277).
instrument.key_provisions: The Contracting Powers agree to abstain from the use of bullets which expand or flatten easily in the human body, such as bullets with a hard envelope which does not entirely cover the core or is pierced with incisions (operative para. 1). The Declaration binds only Contracting Powers in a war between two or more of them (operative para. 2) and ceases to be binding once a non-contracting Power joins one of the belligerents (operative para. 3). It is subject to ratification, with deposit at The Hague (operative paras. 4 to 6); non-signatory Powers may adhere by notification to the Netherlands Government (operative para. 7); denunciation takes effect one year after written notification and affects only the notifying Power (operative paras. 8 and 9). The preamble invokes the sentiments of the 1868 St Petersburg Declaration.
instrument.behavior_change: Delegates described the rule as directed at bullets already made and used. Colonel Gilinsky (Russia) said the formula aimed, as at St Petersburg in 1868, to prohibit bullets that already existed, and that the dumdum had been used in two wars (Proceedings, 1899, pp. 83-84, 279). General Sir John Ardagh (Great Britain) said the dumdum had been made in India because the fully jacketed Lee-Metford bullet did not stop a determined enemy, and asked for liberty to modify jacket or core (pp. 276-278). Captain Crozier (United States) said the United States was satisfied with its bullet, and Mr White stated that the United States had not used and did not intend to use any bullet other than those of other civilized nations (pp. 80, 84, 85). Great Britain, the Power whose bullet was discussed, adhered only on 30 August 1907 (Trb. 1966, 233). Whether British service ammunition changed in consequence was not established in the sources reviewed.
instrument.historical_background: Russia's circular of 30 December 1898 (11 January 1899, new style) proposed, as point 2, banning new firearms and new explosives (Scott 1915, pp. xvi-xvii). In the First Commission's military subcommission the Swiss delegate, Colonel Kunzli, raised the dumdum bullet on 26 May 1899, the Netherlands sought its prohibition, and a Russian formula, reworded by the Russian, French and Romanian delegates, was adopted on 31 May by 19 votes to 1 (Great Britain), Austria-Hungary abstaining. The First Commission upheld it on 22 June by 20 votes to 2 (Great Britain and the United States), Portugal abstaining, after rejecting Captain Crozier's general formula as too vague. The plenary Conference adopted it on 21 July against the votes of the United States and Great Britain, and 15 Powers signed the Declaration at the closing meeting on 29 July 1899 (Proceedings, 1899, pp. 79-87, 221, 276-280, 332-344).

provisions.provision: Prohibit use of bullets which expand or flatten easily in the human body
provisions.bound_parties_detail: Every Contracting Power on identical terms ("The Contracting Parties agree to abstain"; French "Les Puissances contractantes s'interdisent")
provisions.geographic_scope: No geographic limit; applies in a war between two or more Contracting Powers
provisions.exceptions: Binding only in a war between two or more Contracting Powers (operative para. 2); ceases to be binding once a non-contracting Power joins one of the belligerents (operative para. 3). The two constructions named (hard envelope not entirely covering the core; envelope pierced with incisions) are examples ("such as"); the rule is defined by the bullet expanding or flattening easily in the human body. At signature on 27 July 1899 the Greek delegate, Mr Delyanni, declared that Greece signed with the express reservation that the Gras rifle bullet then in Greek service was not included (Proceedings, 1899, p. 213); the depositary records no reservation for Greece and Scott (1915) records none. The text does not address development, production or possession.
provisions.text_or_paraphrase: The Contracting Parties agree to abstain from the use of bullets which expand or flatten easily in the human body, such as bullets with a hard envelope which does not entirely cover the core or is pierced with incisions.
provisions.locator: Operative para. 1 (French: "Les Puissances contractantes s'interdisent l'emploi de balles qui s'épanouissent ou s'aplatissent facilement dans le corps humain, telles que les balles à enveloppe dure dont l'enveloppe ne couvrirait pas entièrement le noyau ou serait pourvue d'incisions."). Entry into force from the Netherlands treaty database (4 September 1900); no termination recorded.

events.event: Russian circular proposes banning new firearms and explosives
events.actors: Russia (Foreign Minister Count Muraviev)
events.attribution: Circular printed in Scott, The Hague Conventions and Declarations of 1899 and 1907 (1915)
events.description: The second Russian circular listed the subjects for the conference. Point 2 proposed the "interdiction of the employment in armies and fleets of new firearms of every description and of new explosives". The bullet question was taken up under this heading in the military subcommission.

events.event: Swiss delegate raises the dumdum bullet in the military subcommission
events.actors: First subcommission of the First Commission; Switzerland (Colonel Kunzli); Netherlands (General den Beer Poortugael); Great Britain (General Sir John Ardagh)
events.attribution: Minutes of the first subcommission, first meeting, in Scott (ed.), Proceedings of the Hague Peace Conferences: Conference of 1899 (1920)
events.description: Colonel Kunzli asked whether projectiles which aggravate wounds should be prohibited, saying he had the dumdum bullet in view. General den Beer Poortugael said his Government had authorized him to ask for the absolute prohibition of dumdum bullets and similar projectiles. Sir John Ardagh said there must be a misunderstanding, as dumdum bullets were ordinary projectiles.

events.event: Russian bullet formula tabled; delegations state positions
events.actors: First subcommission; Russia (Colonel Gilinsky); Switzerland (Colonel Kunzli); France (General Mounier); United States (Captain Crozier); Great Britain (Sir John Ardagh)
events.attribution: Minutes of the first subcommission, second meeting, in Scott (ed.), Proceedings of the Hague Peace Conferences: Conference of 1899 (1920)
events.description: Colonel Gilinsky read the Russian proposal to prohibit bullets whose envelope does not entirely cover the core at the point or is pierced with incisions, and in general bullets which expand or flatten easily in the human body. Kunzli withdrew his own text. Most delegations accepted the Russian proposal, several with General Mounier's request for more general wording; Captain Crozier thought his Government would endorse Gilinsky's ideas, and Sir John Ardagh accepted ad referendum. The Russian, French and Romanian delegates were asked to submit a final text.

events.event: Military subcommission adopts the bullet text by 19 votes to 1
events.actors: First subcommission; Great Britain (Sir John Ardagh); Austria-Hungary (Lieutenant Colonel von Khuepach); Russia (Colonel Gilinsky, Mr Raffalovich)
events.attribution: Minutes of the first subcommission, third meeting, in Scott (ed.), Proceedings of the Hague Peace Conferences: Conference of 1899 (1920)
events.description: Von Khuepach proposed a general prohibition of bullets causing uselessly cruel wounds. Ardagh supported him and asked for liberty to use projectiles of sufficient efficacy against "savages"; Raffalovich and Gilinsky rejected a distinction between enemies, and the President said none should be made. The Russian-French-Romanian text was adopted by 19 votes (including the United States) to 1 (Great Britain), Austria-Hungary abstaining. Later in the meeting the word "explosive" was added to the definition.

events.event: First Commission upholds the text by 20 votes to 2
events.actors: First Commission; Great Britain (Sir John Ardagh); United States (Captain Crozier); Russia (Colonel Gilinsky); Germany (Colonel Gross von Schwarzhoff); Portugal (Count de Macedo)
events.attribution: Minutes of the First Commission, third meeting, in Scott (ed.), Proceedings of the Hague Peace Conferences: Conference of 1899 (1920)
events.description: Ardagh read a declaration defending the dumdum bullet as necessary to stop a determined enemy and objecting to the technical details of construction in the text. Crozier proposed instead to forbid "bullets which inflict uselessly cruel wounds ... and in general every kind of bullet which exceeds the limit necessary in order to put a man hors de combat at once"; the President, den Beer Poortugael and Gilinsky called it too vague. Gross von Schwarzhoff said the German army had never considered a bullet with an uncovered core. The original text was upheld by 20 votes to 2 (England and the United States), Portugal abstaining.

events.event: First Commission drops a five-year term for the bullet rule
events.actors: First Commission; reporter (Jonkheer van Karnebeek); Russia (Colonel Gilinsky, Mr Martens); Romania (Mr Beldiman); United States (Captain Mahan)
events.attribution: Minutes of the First Commission, seventh meeting, in Scott (ed.), Proceedings of the Hague Peace Conferences: Conference of 1899 (1920)
events.description: The reporter proposed extending the St Petersburg Declaration to the three points for five years, partly to meet the objections of the two Governments that had not joined the bullet vote. Mahan and Captain Scheine objected that a five-year term would change the scope of the gas and bullet votes, and Gilinsky insisted that the bullet prohibition should continue indefinitely. The proposal was not pursued.

events.event: First Commission votes 16 to 2 on the bullet point
events.actors: First Commission; United States; Great Britain; Portugal
events.attribution: Minutes of the First Commission, eighth meeting, in Scott (ed.), Proceedings of the Hague Peace Conferences: Conference of 1899 (1920)
events.description: The Commission decided to propose a separate declaration or convention on each point and adopted the third point by 16 votes to 2 (United States and Great Britain), Portugal abstaining.

events.event: Plenary Conference adopts the bullet engagement
events.actors: Plenary Conference; United States (Captain Crozier, Mr White, Captain Mahan, Mr Low); Great Britain (Sir Julian Pauncefote); Russia (Colonel Gilinsky); Netherlands (Jonkheer van Karnebeek, General den Beer Poortugael)
events.attribution: Minutes of the sixth plenary meeting, in Scott (ed.), Proceedings of the Hague Peace Conferences: Conference of 1899 (1920)
events.description: Crozier moved his general formula as an amendment, arguing that the text covered one detail of construction and condemned the dumdum without evidence; Pauncefote supported him. White proposed referral back to the Commission, which was rejected by 20 votes to 5 (United States, Denmark, Great Britain, Greece, Portugal). Priority for the American formula was refused by 17 votes to 8 (United States, Belgium, China, Denmark, Great Britain, Greece, Portugal, Serbia). The Commission's formula was then adopted unanimously except for the United States and Great Britain, Portugal abstaining and Luxembourg absent.

events.event: Final Act lists the Declaration as a separate act open to signature
events.actors: Plenary Conference; Drafting Committee (reporter Louis Renault)
events.attribution: Minutes of the seventh plenary meeting, in Scott (ed.), Proceedings of the Hague Peace Conferences: Conference of 1899 (1920)
events.description: The Conference approved the Final Act, under which the Conventions and the three Declarations form separate acts, dated the day of signature, which may be signed until 31 December 1899. Renault noted that the title of the bullet Declaration had been completed by restoring the clause on hard envelopes, which did not change the substance.
events.locator: Seventh plenary meeting, p. 103 (page inferred from the neighbouring running head)

events.event: Final texts adopted; Greek reservation and British letter
events.actors: Plenary Conference; Louis Renault; Greece (Mr Delyanni); Great Britain (Sir Julian Pauncefote)
events.attribution: Minutes of the eighth plenary meeting and note to the sixth meeting, in Scott (ed.), Proceedings of the Hague Peace Conferences: Conference of 1899 (1920)
events.description: Renault presented the common preamble and final clauses, explaining that the reference to St Petersburg did not imply adhesion to the 1868 Declaration, and the Conference adopted the texts. Delyanni declared that Greece would sign with the express reservation that the Gras rifle bullet still in Greek service was not included. By a letter of the same day Pauncefote informed the President that, in view of the plenary vote of 21 July, his Government would not insert the declaration on dumdum bullets it had announced.
events.locator: Eighth plenary meeting, pp. 211-213; note to sixth meeting, p. 82 n. 1

events.event: Declaration adopted and signed at The Hague
events.actors: Belgium, Bulgaria, Denmark, France, Greece, Mexico, Montenegro, Netherlands, Persia, Romania, Russia, Siam, Spain, Sweden and Norway, Turkey
events.attribution: Table of signatures read at the closing meeting, in Scott (ed.), Proceedings of the Hague Peace Conferences: Conference of 1899 (1920); Netherlands treaty database; ICRC
events.description: The Declaration is dated 29 July 1899, the date of the Final Act. The table of signatures read at the closing meeting lists 15 Powers as having signed it that day; the same 15 sign the French original reproduced in UK Treaty Series 1907, No. 32. The United States, Great Britain and Portugal did not sign.
events.locator: Closing meeting, p. 221; text and signature blocks, pp. 262-264

events.event: Signature open until 31 December 1899
events.actors: Powers represented at the Conference
events.attribution: Final Act, as reported at the seventh plenary meeting, in Scott (ed.), Proceedings of the Hague Peace Conferences: Conference of 1899 (1920)
events.description: Under the Final Act the Declaration could be signed until 31 December 1899. Austria-Hungary, China, Germany, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, the Kingdom of Serbia and Switzerland are not in the closing-meeting list but appear as signatories in the depositary record, which gives every signature the date of the act; their actual signature dates were not established.
events.locator: Seventh plenary meeting, p. 103; table of signatures, p. 268

events.event: British minister reports expanding bullets used by Boers
events.actors: United Kingdom (General Laurie MP; Mr Powell-Williams for the War Office); South African Republic; Orange Free State
events.attribution: House of Commons debate, 1 March 1900 (Hansard, vol. 79, cols 1415-1416)
events.description: Answering a question citing a report by Lord Roberts that six men had been wounded by Mauser bullets with slits cut in the jacket, the War Office stated that this was the first official intimation of the use of such expansive bullets by the Boers and that no understanding on such bullets had been reached with the two Republics. Neither Great Britain nor the Boer republics was then bound by the Declaration; the exchange is recorded as context, not as an allegation under it.

events.event: First deposit of ratifications and entry into force
events.actors: Austria-Hungary, Belgium, Bulgaria, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, Persia, Romania, Russia, Siam, Spain, Sweden and Norway
events.attribution: Netherlands treaty database; Netherlands Treaty Series (Trb. 1966, 233); ICRC
events.description: The depositary and the ICRC give entry into force on 4 September 1900. Trb. 1966, 233 states that the provisions entered into force on that date for the states that had ratified by then. The ICRC gives Denmark and Spain 4 November 1900; the depositary database, Trb. 1966, 233, the 1905 Dutch royal order and Scott (1915) give 4 September 1900.
events.locator: Treaty data: entry into force 04-09-1900; Trb. 1966, 233, sections E and G

events.event: China deposits its ratification
events.actors: China
events.attribution: Netherlands treaty database; ICRC; Dutch royal order of 23 January 1905 (FRUS 1905)
events.description: China's ratification was deposited on 21 November 1904, the last by a signatory other than Turkey.

events.event: Dutch royal order publishes the list of ratifications
events.actors: Netherlands (Queen Wilhelmina; Foreign Minister Melvil van Lynden)
events.attribution: Royal order of 23 January 1905 (Staatsblad 1905, no. 29), translation enclosed in a despatch from the United States chargé at The Hague, FRUS 1905
events.description: The order lists the Powers for which the 1899 acts were obligatory on 31 December 1904. For Declaration IV,3 it lists 22 ratifying Powers, including Montenegro (16 October 1900); it marks Great Britain, Portugal and the United States as having neither signed nor ratified and Turkey as having signed but not ratified.

events.event: Norway and Sweden listed as parties by succession
events.actors: Norway; Sweden
events.attribution: Netherlands treaty database (parties table)
events.description: The depositary database lists Norway and Sweden separately with consent type "Su" (succession) and entry into force on 17 June 1905, beside the entry for the Kingdom of Sweden and Norway. The basis of the entries and their date were not established; Scott (1915) and the 1905 royal order list only Sweden and Norway.

events.event: Turkey deposits its ratification
events.actors: Turkey
events.attribution: Netherlands treaty database; Trb. 1966, 233; Scott (1915)
events.description: Turkey, which had signed on 29 July 1899, deposited its ratification on 12 June 1907, completing ratification by all signatory Powers (Scott 1915, p. 228).

events.event: Portugal adheres
events.actors: Portugal
events.attribution: Trb. 1966, 233; Scott (1915); Netherlands treaty database
events.description: Portugal, which had abstained in the votes of 22 June, 20 July and 21 July 1899 and did not sign, adhered under operative para. 7 on 29 August 1907.

events.event: Great Britain adheres
events.actors: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland (Sir Henry Howard); Netherlands (Foreign Minister van Tets van Goudriaan)
events.attribution: UK Treaty Series 1907, No. 32; Trb. 1966, 233; Netherlands treaty database
events.description: The British Minister at The Hague notified the accession of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland to the Declaration on 30 August 1907, by a note separate from the same-day accession to the gas Declaration (IV,2); the Netherlands Foreign Minister acknowledged both notes on 3 September 1907 and undertook to inform the other Contracting Powers. Great Britain had voted against the text throughout 1899 and did not sign.
events.locator: Nos. 1 and 3 and Annex I, pp. 1-5

events.event: Nicaragua adheres
events.actors: Nicaragua
events.attribution: Trb. 1966, 233; Scott (1915); Netherlands treaty database
events.description: Nicaragua adhered under operative para. 7 on 11 October 1907.

events.event: German Emperor alleges Allied use of dumdum bullets
events.actors: Germany (Emperor William II); France; United Kingdom
events.attribution: Telegram from the Emperor to President Wilson, forwarded by Ambassador Gerard, FRUS 1914, Supplement
events.description: The Emperor stated that after taking Longwy his troops had found thousands of dumdum cartridges "made by special government machinery", and that such ammunition had been found on French dead, wounded and prisoners and on British troops; he described their use as "strictly forbidden by the established rules of international law" and protested. The telegram does not name the Declaration. Germany, France and the United Kingdom were parties (Netherlands treaty database).

events.event: French President denies the charge and accuses Germany
events.actors: France (President Poincaré); Germany
events.attribution: Telegram from President Poincaré to President Wilson, FRUS 1914, Supplement
events.description: Poincaré called the German claim that dumdum bullets were made in a French Government shop and used by French soldiers a calumny and "a bold attempt to reverse the charges", and stated that Germany had been using dumdum bullets since the beginning of the war; he said France had denounced German outrages to the powers signatory of the Hague convention from 18 August.

events.event: United States declines to judge the dumdum charges
events.actors: United States (President Wilson; Secretary of State Bryan; Ambassador Gerard)
events.attribution: FRUS 1914, Supplement
events.description: Gerard forwarded specimens of alleged dumdum bullets at the German Government's request and advised keeping out of the controversy (14 September). Bryan replied that no action would be taken and that the President did not discuss the merits (18 September). Wilson told Poincaré on 19 September that the truth could be impartially determined when the conflict was over. No formal finding on the dumdum charges was identified in the sources reviewed.

events.event: Ethiopia adheres
events.actors: Ethiopia
events.attribution: Trb. 1966, 233; Netherlands treaty database; ICRC
events.description: Ethiopia adhered under operative para. 7 on 9 August 1935.

events.event: Soviet Union recognises the Hague Declarations ratified by Russia
events.actors: USSR
events.attribution: Netherlands treaty database (declaration text); Trb. 1981, 95
events.description: The USSR recognised the 1899 and 1907 Hague Conventions and Declarations ratified by Russia to the extent that they do not conflict with the UN Charter and have not been amended or superseded by later agreements to which the USSR is a party. The depositary records the entry under the Russian Federation.

events.event: German Democratic Republic declares renewed application
events.actors: German Democratic Republic
events.description: By a note of 22 December 1958, received by the Netherlands Foreign Ministry on 9 February 1959, the GDR declared that it again applied the Declaration, except for provisions contrary to the UN Charter or amended or replaced by later agreements to which it belonged. The Netherlands did not then recognise the GDR. The current depositary database lists no GDR entry.

events.event: Rome Statute lists expanding bullets as a war crime
events.actors: United Nations Diplomatic Conference of Plenipotentiaries on the Establishment of an International Criminal Court
events.attribution: Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (ICC consolidated text)
events.description: Article 8(2)(b)(xix) lists as a war crime in international armed conflict "Employing bullets which expand or flatten easily in the human body, such as bullets with a hard envelope which does not entirely cover the core or is pierced with incisions", repeating the Declaration's wording. Any relationship to this Declaration is coded on the later instrument.

events.event: Kampala amendment extends the war crime to non-international conflict
events.actors: Review Conference of the Rome Statute
events.attribution: Rome Statute (ICC consolidated text), footnote to Art. 8(2)(e)
events.description: Resolution RC/Res.5 of 11 June 2010 inserted Article 8(2)(e)(xv), which lists the same conduct as a war crime in armed conflicts not of an international character, for the States Parties that accept the amendment.

events.event: Ukraine confirms succession
events.actors: Ukraine
events.attribution: Netherlands treaty database
events.description: Ukraine confirmed the validity for it, by succession from 24 August 1991, of the 1899 and 1907 Hague Conventions and Declarations recognised by the USSR in the format and scope of the Soviet note of 7 March 1955.

overview_md: The Hague Declaration (IV,3) of 29 July 1899 commits its parties to abstain from the use of bullets which expand or flatten easily in the human body, such as bullets with a hard envelope which does not entirely cover the core or is pierced with incisions ([ICRC](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/ihl-treaties/hague-decl-iv-3-1899)). It was one of three declarations adopted at the First Hague Peace Conference, alongside those on balloons and asphyxiating gases. Delegates identified the British "dumdum" bullet as the bullet in view, and Great Britain and the United States voted against the text ([Proceedings, 1899](https://archive.org/details/proceedingsofhag1899inteuoft), pp. 79-87). Twenty-three Powers signed it (counting Sweden and Norway once) and all had ratified by 1907; Portugal and Great Britain adhered in August 1907, Nicaragua in 1907 and Ethiopia in 1935 ([Trb. 1966, 233](https://zoek.officielebekendmakingen.nl/trb-1966-233.pdf)). The United States neither signed nor adhered. The Declaration binds only in wars between parties and ceases to bind once a non-party joins a belligerent. It entered into force on 4 September 1900 and has no fixed term; the depositary and the ICRC treat it as in force, and the depositary database lists 35 present-day parties, several of them by succession ([Netherlands treaty database](https://treatydatabase.overheid.nl/en/Treaty/Details/002423_p.html)). Its wording reappears in Article 8(2)(b)(xix) of the 1998 Rome Statute, and the ICRC customary law study states the rule as Rule 77.
provisions_md:
The Declaration has no numbered articles. Citations refer to the preamble, nine operative paragraphs and the closing formula of the [authentic French text](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/fr/ihl-treaties/hague-decl-iv-3-1899/declaration), checked against [Scott, Les Conventions et Déclarations de La Haye (1918)](https://archive.org/details/lesconventionset00laha), pp. 227-228, and the French original printed in [UK Treaty Series 1907, No. 32](https://treaties.fcdo.gov.uk/data/Library2/pdf/1907-TS0032.pdf); the [English translation](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/ihl-treaties/hague-decl-iv-3-1899/declaration) follows the same order.

### Preamble
- The plenipotentiaries declare themselves inspired by the sentiments expressed in the St Petersburg Declaration of 29 November (11 December) 1868. Louis Renault told the Conference that this wording did not imply adhesion to the 1868 Declaration ([Proceedings, 1899](https://archive.org/details/proceedingsofhag1899inteuoft), p. 211).

### The prohibition
- The Contracting Powers agree to abstain from the use of bullets which expand or flatten easily in the human body (operative para. 1).
- Two constructions are given as examples: bullets with a hard envelope which does not entirely cover the core, and bullets whose envelope is pierced with incisions. The words "such as" make them illustrations; the defining test is easy expansion or flattening in the body.
- The text names no bullet. Colonel Gilinsky (Russia) said it would be for each government to decide whether a given projectile fell within the formula; delegates and the reports referred to the British "dumdum" bullet (Proceedings, pp. 83-84).
- The rule concerns use in war. The text does not address development, production, possession or police use.

### Bound parties and the general participation clause
- The Declaration binds Contracting Powers identically, but only in a war between two or more of them (operative para. 2).
- It ceases to be binding once a non-contracting Power joins one of the belligerents (operative para. 3).
- On 27 July 1899, before signature, the Greek delegate declared that he would sign with the express reservation that the Gras rifle bullet then in Greek service was not included (Proceedings, p. 213); the depositary records no reservation.

### Duration
- No term is stated; the obligation is not time-limited, unlike the five-year balloon Declaration (IV,1) signed the same day.

### Final clauses
- Ratification as soon as possible, deposit at The Hague, and a proces-verbal of each deposit sent to all Contracting Powers (operative paras. 4 to 6).
- Non-signatory Powers may adhere by written notification to the Netherlands Government (operative para. 7).
- Denunciation takes effect one year after written notification to the Netherlands Government and affects only the notifying Power (operative paras. 8 and 9).
- The text contains no provisions on information exchange, verification, consultation, dispute settlement or enforcement.
participation_md:
- **Signature.** The Declaration is dated 29 July 1899. Fifteen Powers signed at the closing meeting that day; under the Final Act signature remained open until 31 December 1899, and eight more Powers appear as signatories ([Proceedings, 1899](https://archive.org/details/proceedingsofhag1899inteuoft), pp. 103, 221 and 268). Their actual signature dates were not established; the depositary records all signatures under 29 July 1899.
- **Ratification and entry into force.** Ratifications were deposited at The Hague. The Declaration entered into force on 4 September 1900 for the Powers that had ratified by then and later for each subsequent ratifying or acceding state on its date of deposit or accession ([Trb. 1966, 233](https://zoek.officielebekendmakingen.nl/trb-1966-233.pdf)). Turkey was the last signatory to ratify, on 12 June 1907.
- **Adhesion.** Open to non-signatory Powers (operative para. 7). Portugal (29 August 1907), Great Britain (30 August 1907, [UK Treaty Series 1907, No. 32](https://treaties.fcdo.gov.uk/data/Library2/pdf/1907-TS0032.pdf)), Nicaragua (11 October 1907) and Ethiopia (9 August 1935) adhered.
- **Succession.** The [depositary database](https://treatydatabase.overheid.nl/en/Treaty/Details/002423_p.html) lists entries by succession for Norway and Sweden (1905), Austria and Hungary (1918), India and Pakistan (1950), Fiji (1973), South Africa (1978), Serbia (2001), Montenegro (2007) and Ukraine (2015), and records declarations by the USSR (1955) and Belarus (1962) recognising the Hague acts ratified by Russia, subject to conditions ([Trb. 1981, 95](https://zoek.officielebekendmakingen.nl/trb-1981-95.pdf)).
- **Participants.** 23 signatories, all of which ratified (counting Sweden and Norway once). The depositary database lists 35 present-day parties, checked 12 October 2026; the [ICRC](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/ihl-treaties/hague-decl-iv-3-1899/state-parties) lists 33, without India and Pakistan. Neither the current depositary database nor the ICRC lists Montenegro's 1900 ratification, which appears in Trb. 1966, 233 and the 1905 Dutch list ([FRUS 1905, doc. 704](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1905/d704)). The United States is not a party.
- **Duration.** No term; in force according to the depositary and the ICRC.
- **Withdrawal.** Denunciation on one year's written notice to the Netherlands Government (operative paras. 8 and 9); none recorded.
- **Amendment and review.** No amendment procedure and no review conferences.
- **Depositary.** The Government of the Netherlands.

### Origins
Russia's circular of 30 December 1898 (11 January 1899, new style) proposed banning new firearms and new explosives ([Scott 1915](https://archive.org/details/hagueconventions00inteuoft), pp. xvi-xvii). In the military subcommission of the First Commission on 26 May 1899 the Swiss delegate, Colonel Kunzli, raised the dumdum bullet, and General den Beer Poortugael said the Netherlands Government sought its prohibition; General Sir John Ardagh (Great Britain) replied that dumdums were ordinary projectiles ([Proceedings, 1899](https://archive.org/details/proceedingsofhag1899inteuoft), p. 332). On 29 May Colonel Gilinsky tabled the Russian formula, which the Russian, French and Romanian delegates then reworded (pp. 338-339).

### Negotiation
On 31 May Ardagh asked for liberty to use effective projectiles against "savage" enemies; Mr Raffalovich (Russia) and the President rejected any distinction between enemies, and the text passed by 19 votes to 1 (Great Britain), Austria-Hungary abstaining (pp. 343-344). In the First Commission on 22 June Ardagh said the dumdum, made in India because the Lee-Metford bullet did not stop a determined enemy, caused no useless suffering, and objected to the construction details. Captain Crozier (United States) proposed instead a general ban on bullets exceeding what is needed to put a man out of action; the President and Gilinsky called it too vague. The text was upheld by 20 votes to 2, Portugal abstaining (pp. 276-280), and by 16 to 2 on 20 July (p. 329). In plenary on 21 July Crozier argued that the text fixed one detail and condemned the dumdum without evidence, and Mr White stated that the United States did not intend to use bullets other than those of other nations. Referral and priority for Crozier's formula were refused, and the text was adopted against the United States and Great Britain, Portugal abstaining (pp. 79-87). Fifteen Powers signed on 29 July (p. 221).

### Later adhesions
Portugal and Great Britain adhered in August 1907 ([UK Treaty Series 1907, No. 32](https://treaties.fcdo.gov.uk/data/Library2/pdf/1907-TS0032.pdf)). The United States remained outside ([FRUS 1905](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1905/d704)).

### Allegations
In March 1900 the War Office told the House of Commons it had its first official report of expanding bullets used by the Boers; neither side was then bound by the Declaration ([Hansard](https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1900/mar/01/expanding-bullets)). In September 1914 Emperor William II alleged French and British use of dumdum cartridges, and President Poincaré denied it and accused Germany ([FRUS 1914 Supp.](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1914Supp/d1260)). President Wilson declined to judge ([FRUS](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1914Supp/d1268)). No formal finding was identified in the sources reviewed.

### Later record
The [ICRC customary law study](https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/customary-ihl/v1/rule77) states Rule 77 as applicable in all armed conflicts and describes United States practice as possibly ambiguous. The [Rome Statute](https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/RS-Eng.pdf) lists the conduct as a war crime (Art. 8(2)(b)(xix); Art. 8(2)(e)(xv) from 2010).

One row per signatory, accession and succession entry.
